title: No Chance of Passing With This Alone
text:
After reading this book cover to cover and subsequently failing the N10-006 in April '16, it became readily apparent that there are a number of very important topics that aren't even mentioned in this book or were simply glossed over as insignificant despite being heavily emphasized on the exam.

The only reason I'm giving this book 3 rather than even fewer stars is that A) there is still a lot of good content with supporting diagrams/images and B) the N10-006 exam has clearly been overhauled in terms of the difficulty level required to pass. While I thought the exam was meant to verify that folks have the necessary core competencies to go into (or in my case continue) a career in networking, that is apparently no longer the case. They are now expecting test takers to demonstrate existing proficiencies in a number of different areas. Further, I honestly think they have folks who do not speak English as their primary language writing some of the questions, and a number of questions have multiple right answers with intentionally misleading phrasing.

For those of you that are on the fence in regards to taking this exam, I would suggest going another route. The exam difficulty is in no way commensurate with its reputation (i.e. looks OK on a resume but nothing that is going to be a deciding factor in getting you a promotion or getting you hired over someone else who doesn't have this cert). It is not worth the $285 for the test, costs of training materials, or your time in studying. I did eventually pass the exam on my second attempt by the skin of my teeth in May '16, but will in no way be interested in renewing the cert when the time comes.

title: Took the class
text:
Last night I took a continuing education class over the subject of this book and met Bobbie Christensen. I really enjoyed the class and it really inspired me to make a plan to write my first book. I have so many ideas floating around for stories, but never knew all the things involved. She went over things that I just never thought about; all the forms and processes you have to go through to publish your book as well as taxes and how to market yourself.

Writing a book is a very personal thing, a very creative process. She is sharing what works for her, it's not the only way to get your ideas out there, but it is her way. I love that she offers her opinions and help in her book; in the first few pages she gives out her email for anyone to contact her with questions.

You take her suggestions and move them around to fit you. If you are really serious about being a writer, this book offers one way to make that dream happen. Take what you will from this book then do some other research; the more you know, the better equipped you are to handle things.

Make this book apart of your research, but don't end there. Explore all avenues and see what works best for you. If you like a step by step explanation of the writing to publishing to marketing process, this book is a good pick for you.

title: Not worth the money just for the historical perspective
text:
The first of the two stories is amusing in its humor and interesting from an historical point of view. As soon as the reader gets past the first chapter you start to notice subtle incongruencies, this because the original story was written in 1959. It offers some insights into what was considered to be acceptable and normal at the time in Sci-FI as a genre and in America as a whole. Many of the comments and assumptions the author makes would be considered blatantly chauvinistic and insulting to women by today's standards. Which is not to say that the author is a chauvinist just that what was acceptable in 1959 is not acceptable by today's standards. As one reads you can find many of these cultural incongruencies that serve to illustrate may of the changes in America in the past 41 years.
As far as entertainment goes this is an amusing, lighthearted and funny story although the writing can, at times, seem a bit overly simple. As a long time Poul Anderson fan I can recommend "Virgin Planet" as a stand-alone story. What I cannot recommend is "Star Ways" it has all of he bad points of "Virgin Planet" without the saving sense of humor.
When taken as a whole I am sorry I spent the money and so will you if you do too.

title: Nasreen's Secret School: A True Story from Afghanistan
text:
ISBN 1416994378 - Manufactured in China. Ages 6 to 9. I can't really say what I expected from this book. Something like a Little House on the Prairie tale set in Afghanistan, perhaps? Or a 1930s-esque story of the fight for equal rights for women? Whatever it was, I've forgotten it. What I actually got was good enough to erase the pre-conceived notion from my mind!

Nasreen and her parents live with her grandmother. The Taliban has come to power and they've destroyed much that was beautiful about their city, Herat. Art, music and learning fade and, far worse, are prohibited to females. Young girls are not allowed to learn as their mothers and grandmothers had learned. When Nasreen's father was taken away by the Taliban, her mother went to search for him. Missing her parents and not allowed to be outside alone, Nasreen falls silent and withdraws. Her grandmother hears about a secret school for girls and hopes that attending will help Nasreen. Even though it's against the law, the girls, the teachers, the parents and even the neighborhood boys quietly fight against the Taliban's ban on education for girls. Her grandmother hopes it's enough to give Nasreen a sense of hope and bring her back to life.

The great amount of white space around the images seems, at first, to be a waste of space. It appears unattractive and left me feeling that the images should have been larger. That impression passed quickly and I really began to FEEL that white space. Nasreen's story and the city of Herat under the Taliban has a desolate, empty and somewhat lonely feel that, weirdly, is conveyed by these vast expanses of white surrounding small illustrations and minimal text. The images themselves are incredibly colorful and range from somewhat scary (when Nasreen's father is taken) to beautiful (as Nasreen learns). I loved the inclusion of a Bamiyan Buddha and Little Red Riding Hood - diversity rocks!

In this age, it's hard to say that this book is strictly age appropriate. Parents, in an effort to protect their children, are sometimes apt to overdo it when it comes to books. I'd urge those parents to consider this book anyway. Read it yourself first, of course. The problem isn't the vocabulary. While there might be a few words that are above the heads of six year olds, that's a good thing. Reading, after all, is about learning! The thing that I suspect some parents will worry about is the potential for upsetting their children with the fact that Nasreen's parents are gone, and the implied violence of the Taliban. It is worth taking the time to talk about those things. Children learn empathy and it's not too soon for that. If, for your child, you feel it IS, pass this one by for now.

Most important is the message, which is fantastic: education is worth fighting for. In the U.S., we know this, but it's good to be reminded every now and then with a tale more modern than [[ASIN:034551100X A Mighty Long Way: My Journey to Justice at Little Rock Central High School]]. That the sale of the book benefits The Global Fund for Children is a bonus to me and the author's note in the front of the book puts the story in context for adults and older readers.

- AnnaLovesBooks

title: voices from the internal diaspora
text:
When the Romans destroyed the temple of Jerusalem, crushed Jewish resistance, and sent the survivors into exile, nobody could have predicted that the exiles would treasure their language, their culture, and their religious identity for nearly two thousand years. Some dreamed of their old land during their times of troubles, others assimilated to the lands of exile. They became "others" but at the same time remained Jews. They mixed with Romans, Teutons, Slavs, Arabs, Iranians and Ethiopians, to name a few, but kept that separate identity as well. Everybody knows what finally happened---it's the Mother of All Property Disputes. As a descendant of that people, I have always looked at the Native Americans with considerable empathy. Though they didn't lose every shred of their land in many cases, they were otherwise "taken to the cleaners", even villainized for trying to defend their own land, condemned to live at the bottom of the American heap. If modern Indians are bitter about this, if they don't love the Stars and Stripes, who could blame them ? The astonishing thing is that so many do accept their citizenship. Deep inside though, the survivors of the American genocide cling to the land, to the sense of belonging here, to an identity which marks them as separate. At the same time, their families too have mingled and assimilated, so condemning "whites" or "blacks" can often be equivalent to condemning a part of oneself. How can individuals come to terms with such ambivalence ? I TELL YOU NOW is a collection of 18 short autobiographies by Native American poets and writers. Though a sense of alienation and of being people apart flows through the book, the different takes on being Indian in the USA are nearly as many as the writers. Some are angry, some hurt by life circumstances more than by prejudice, yet others pursue successful careers, while others have fought self-destructive habits for years. Poetry runs through the book---each chapter includes some of the author's verses---as does love of the land and the feeling of being connected to it. Some writers were reluctant to focus too much on themselves, having been taught to avoid the limelight, to be modest and self-effacing. This is culturally understandable, but if you refuse to write about yourself, you can't really write autobiography ! We'll have to conclude that it's a European-derived form, not necessarily one which appeals to Native Americans. Still, the shy response tells us about modern Indian cultures too. Given the way the USA is going, will the Native Americans have to wait so long to get their lands back ? Probably not. But will the lands be still inhabitable ? The big question.

Though I found the book interesting, it is rather too choppy to be a five star book. Participation by people who didn't want to participate also dulls the edge quite a bit. You just start to think about the person who is writing, start to wonder about their experience, thoughts and personality, and the chapter is over. For those who are really into Native American literature, the authors may be familiar. I had not heard of most of them, so started from scratch each time. If a reader is more familiar with the present condition of each native nation, it would help as well, since a New Englander like me has little contact or experience with the native peoples of Alaska, Oklahoma, New Mexico, etc. In short, I TELL YOU NOW stems from a good idea, but perhaps the execution leaves something to be desired.

text: This book hasn’t really captured my attention at this point.  I got this for my daughter for a school book report and I think she has been enjoying it but doesn’t seem very swept away with it at this point either. I think it will pick up as we get further into the book.
